title: Poland, 1939: five dates, different kinds of change
subtitle: An introduction to the first Ostfront Atlas timeline
author: Robert M. Dobo
body:
On September 30, 1939, Poland’s ambassador in Washington rejected a treaty that Germany and the Soviet Union had signed two days earlier. Jerzy Potocki informed the United States that his government would not recognize their division of Polish territory and would work to recover it. Warsaw had surrendered; the Polish state had not accepted its own extinction. That contradiction runs through this collection. The invaders acquired the power to occupy towns, imprison soldiers, expel families, and issue decrees. They could not make those acts into a settlement accepted by the country they had attacked. [1] The five dated studies follow the conversion of diplomatic opportunity into military conquest and then into occupation. The August pact made aggression easier; the invasions of September 1 and 17 destroyed Poland’s room for maneuver; the September 28 treaty revised the invaders’ bargain; and the October 26 administrative change gave German rule a more durable institutional form. These were connected decisions, each with consequences that its makers could influence but never entirely control. Reading them together explains how a state could lose effective government over its territory while its people continued to fight, flee, organize, and seek protection. The country at the center of this struggle was larger and more diverse than a present-day map of Poland suggests. Restored to independence in 1918, it extended well to the east of its current frontier. The Treaty of Riga, signed on March 18, 1921, settled the Polish–Soviet border after war. Polish, Ukrainian, Belarusian, and Jewish communities, among others, lived in its eastern provinces. National identity intersected with religion, class, locality, and conflicting memories of government. Such differences help explain the varied responses to invasion. They did not authorize Berlin or Moscow to dispose of the population or its territory. [2] [3]

August 23: bargaining over other countries

The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact changed the strategic conditions under which Germany could attack Poland. Its public provisions promised nonaggression between Germany and the Soviet Union, consultation and the avoidance of support for a third power fighting either signatory. Those promises mattered because they reduced the immediate danger that Hitler’s attack would bring Soviet opposition. Yet the published treaty was only one part of the transaction. The governments also negotiated a secret protocol dealing with territories whose inhabitants and representatives had no part in the agreement. [4] For Poland, the protocol described an approximate division of interests along the Narew, Vistula and San rivers, leaving open whether any independent Polish state would remain. Its wider provisions concerned the Baltic states, Finland and Bessarabia. This was a framework for disposing of other countries’ futures, rather than a record of territory already conquered. It neither placed Soviet soldiers inside Poland on August 23 nor established the final occupation boundary reached later in September. [5] The pact’s immediate significance lay in the choices it enabled. Hitler could attack Poland with less fear of Soviet intervention against Germany; Stalin acquired opportunities for expansion without committing the Red Army to the opening German attack. Neither advantage made the subsequent course of events inevitable. Britain and France still had to decide whether to fight, and Moscow still had to choose when and how to intervene. The [study of the pact](/articles/molotov-ribbentrop-pact-1939-08-23) reconstructs that diplomatic choice and the separate public and secret documents through which it was expressed. [4] [5]

September 1: military advantage meets resistance

Germany’s invasion turned diplomatic opportunity into an attempt to destroy the Polish armed forces. The geography favored converging attacks: East Prussia supplied an approach from the north, German territory to the west supported the main offensive, and the southern approaches through Slovakia added another threat. Polish commanders faced a difficult choice between defending exposed industrial and population centers and withdrawing toward a shorter position that would surrender them. German strength in armor, aircraft and mobile formations made the problem more urgent, but the outcome still depended on fighting, communications, crossings and the movement of supplies. [6] Polish resistance repeatedly complicated German operations. The Bzura counteroffensive, which began on September 9, forced Germany to respond to a major attack on the flank of its 8th Army. Its eventual defeat shows the limits of a local success when the wider front was collapsing. The military study examines how German mobility, Polish deployment, communications, and supply interacted; an explanation based simply on superior tanks would conceal the decisions and the fighting through which victory was achieved. [7] Britain and France declared war on Germany on September 3, internationalizing the conflict. Chamberlain’s announcement to Parliament explicitly connected British belligerency to Germany’s failure to promise an end to the aggression and withdrawal from Poland. A declaration, however, was different from military relief. The limited French advance in the Saar and the developing British deployment did not remove the immediate pressure on the Polish armies. Their allies were preparing for a prolonged conflict while Poland needed help within days. The [study of September 1](/articles/german-invasion-poland-1939-09-01) follows that mismatch alongside the fighting and the violence inflicted on civilians. [8] [9] [10]

September 17: invasion from the east

The Red Army crossed Poland’s eastern frontier on September 17 while Polish armies were still fighting Germany. Moscow announced that the Polish state had collapsed and presented the invasion as protection for Ukrainians and Belarusians. The Soviet note is evidence of that official justification. Polish authorities were still inside the country when the attack began, and formations continued to resist both invaders. The assertion of state collapse helped Moscow deny its obligations to Poland while sending its forces across a recognized frontier. [11] For the people inside Poland, the second invasion transformed the meaning of the east. A direction of retreat from the German advance became another direction from which hostile forces approached. The Polish leadership crossed into Romania during the night of September 17–18 and was interned; troops sought routes toward Romania and Hungary, while other formations resisted Soviet attacks. Fighting at Grodno and elsewhere showed that the new occupation was imposed, even though the disparity of forces and the existing war against Germany sharply restricted Polish choices. [12] Britain rejected Moscow’s claim that the Polish government had disappeared but did not declare war on the Soviet Union. American ambassador Joseph Kennedy’s report of September 18 records the British distinction between continued recognition of Poland and a further military commitment. For Poland, the practical result was a second invading army without a second allied declaration of war. The [study of the Soviet invasion](/articles/soviet-invasion-poland-1939-09-17) examines the treaty obligations, command decisions, resistance, captivity, and evacuation that shaped this crisis. [13]

Diplomatic continuity

Recognition after territorial defeat

On October 2, U.S. Secretary of State Cordell Hull affirmed that Washington still recognized the Polish government. Recognition maintained diplomatic relations and denied that conquest had extinguished Poland. It could sustain representation abroad; it could not protect a family facing an occupying police force. The September 28 study gives this distinction its full diplomatic context.

[14]

September 28: negotiating the division after invasion

The German–Soviet Boundary and Friendship Treaty revised the August bargain. Its public text declared the agreed boundary definitive and assigned administrative reorganization on either side to the two signatories. The accompanying secret protocol transferred Lithuania into the Soviet sphere, subject to a territorial reservation, while assigning the Lublin province and part of the Warsaw province to Germany. The later partition therefore cannot be read as the straightforward implementation of an unchanged August line. The occupiers were adjusting their arrangement as the military and political situation developed. [15] [16] Warsaw capitulated on the same date, but its surrender and the treaty were separate events. [10] The city’s defenders were ending a siege; the governments in Moscow were asserting the authority to decide Poland’s territorial future. Polish forces continued fighting after Warsaw’s capitulation, and the final major campaign fighting at Kock ended in early October. There was no single moment at which every Polish formation surrendered, every occupation boundary became effective and every political question was settled. [17] Germany and the Soviet Union also tried to determine what Poland’s defeat should mean for the wider war. Their joint declaration called for peace between Germany and the Western powers, treating the results of conquest as a basis for negotiation. Britain and France would have to accept the losses imposed on Poland before Germany’s aggression could be presented as a completed episode. The [study of September 28](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28) follows the territorial revision, repression and population provisions, economic arrangements, and rejection of that proposed settlement. [18]

October 26: making occupation a system of government

The October date concerns the institutions through which Germany governed the territory it controlled. Annexed western and northern districts were incorporated into the Reich, while the General Government under Hans Frank administered another portion of occupied Poland. The latter initially comprised the districts of Kraków, Warsaw, Radom and Lublin. It was an imposed German administration, not a surviving Polish government. The distinction between annexation and the General Government reflected different territorial arrangements within the same project of domination. [19] The General Government’s founding decree bore the date October 12; civilian administration took effect on October 26. Annexation had its own decree and effective date. Those intervals mattered because officials had to determine whose orders would govern a court, workplace, or municipality. The [occupation study](/articles/german-occupation-administration-1939-10-26) follows that process into identification, labor, schools, property, and policing. Its focus is the emerging system at the October changeover, with later measures explicitly identified as subsequent developments. [20] In the Soviet zone, controlled October elections produced assemblies that requested incorporation into the USSR. The union-level incorporation measures followed on November 1–2, after this collection’s final selected date. Annexation therefore cannot be dated simply to the Red Army’s arrival. Nor do electoral proceedings conducted under occupation establish consent. The two occupying regimes differed in their institutions, ideological aims, and methods of persecution. Those differences remain essential even where their policies converged in dismantling independent Polish authority. [21]

The people inside the partition—and the Poland that continued

For civilians, the speed of these changes could defeat even an urgent attempt to escape. Jewish families fled German persecution toward eastern Poland, where the Soviet invasion brought another occupation. The Holocaust Memorial Museum’s account describes refugees struggling with separation, money, shelter, and dangerous crossings. Some tried to return home. Their decisions were made with knowledge of immediate needs and hazards, not knowledge of the later Holocaust. The studies follow these movements alongside military operations because routes open to armies or negotiated between governments were not necessarily safe for a civilian family. [22] The same care is needed when interpreting a welcome, an act of assistance, or an attack on retreating soldiers. Boridczenko’s research on the eastern borderlands examines national, class, and regional attachments together, drawing attention to differences between neighboring localities and to the perspectives of those who recorded them. An individual’s conduct requires evidence about that person and situation. Neither the invaders’ claim to represent a population nor a hostile witness’s description can make an entire ethnic community responsible for the actions of some of its members. [3] Persecution already accompanied conquest and was becoming a system of administration. On September 21, Heydrich instructed security-police commanders to concentrate Jewish populations in selected towns and create Jewish councils compelled to implement German orders. Railway access, census returns, and economic requirements entered the machinery of coercion. This was an early stage of Nazi anti-Jewish policy under occupation; the later extermination system was not yet operating in its completed form. Precise chronology makes the crimes of 1939 visible in their own right and shows how further decisions enlarged them. [23] Polish political continuity required institutions as well as declarations. On September 30, Władysław Raczkiewicz became president and Władysław Sikorski prime minister in France. Within Poland, the Service for Poland’s Victory began organizing clandestine resistance on September 27. These efforts could not reverse military defeat or supply immediate security to the occupied population. They nevertheless kept open political and military alternatives to the future prescribed by the occupying powers. [24] [25]

Reading the maps and the studies together

The dated maps accompany this history by distinguishing political boundaries, territorial control, administrative arrangements, and military movement. A sphere negotiated by diplomats is not territory already occupied; a column passing a crossroads does not establish secure control of the surrounding countryside. Read each arrow and shaded area with its date, legend, and qualification. The retained prewar Polish outline provides a reference against which imposed changes can be compared, without endorsing the claims of the authorities represented. Evidence has different strengths at different scales. A treaty can establish what its signatories agreed; a military report can record a formation’s reported position; testimony can describe what one person encountered. None automatically answers the others’ questions. The linked citations and source-method notes identify these limits. The introduction supplies the common chronology, while the five studies give the negotiations, operations, and occupation measures enough space for their particular causes and consequences to become clear. By late October, the partition had become more than a line negotiated in Moscow. It operated through military custody, restricted movement, confiscated property, compulsory work, and attacks on communities and their leaders. Yet Polish resistance and recognized government abroad continued. The collection follows the decisions that produced this unequal struggle: who acquired power, how they exercised it, and what possibilities remained to the people whose country they had divided.

summary: Five dates trace how diplomatic bargaining became invasion, partition and occupation, while Polish resistance and recognition abroad sustained the state’s claim to independence.
sourceMethod: Numbered citations link claims to treaty texts, dated diplomatic correspondence, documentary scholarship, and historical research. Documents establish their authors’ commitments or reports; German and Soviet justifications are attributed, not adopted. The detailed studies provide fuller evidence for operations, crimes, prisoners, and occupation. This introduction supplies shared chronology and distinctions without treating later events as already complete on the selected dates. Sources were consulted as online texts or preserved project copies; article-specific access details accompany this editorial revision.
